newsitem.title: INDIA: India, China sign pact to reduce border tension.
newsitem.headline: India, China sign pact to reduce border tension.

text.p: India and China on Friday signed an agreement aimed at reducing tensions along their Himalayan frontier, over which they fought a war in 1962.
The agreement on confidence-building measures in military areas along the line of actual control, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, could lead to troop and weapon cutbacks.
Indian officials said the agreement was signed by Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen.
It was signed after 90 minutes of talks between Chinese President Jiang Zemin, the first Chinese president to visit India, and Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told reporters: "The two sides today signed an agreement on confidence-building measures in the military field along the line of actual control in the border areas of India and China.
"They hope this agreement will facilitate consultative agreements between both sides," he added.
The issue of the 4,500 km (2,500 mile) frontier is viewed as central to problems between the two countries, home to one-third of the world's population.
The agreement reaffirmed that "neither side shall use or threaten to use force against the other by any means or seek unilateral military superiority".

"The two sides shall reduce or limit the number of field army, border defence forces, para-military forces and any other mutually agreed category of armed force deployed in mutually agreed geographical zones along the line of actual control to ceilings to be mutually agreed upon," it said.

The agreement said major categories of weapons to be reduced or limited included tanks, infantry combat vehicles, guns, including howitzers, of 75 mm or more, surface-to-surface and surface-to-air missiles and any other system agreed on.
Shen, speaking through an interpreter, said: "When such an agreement is implemented, the number of the armies along this area will be reduced.
"When I refer to the reduction of military personnel, I mean the reduction will depend on the actual conditions.
"If peace and tranquillity are maintained in this area, I don't believe there is any need to maintain a large number of military personnel there," Shen added.
India and China signed an agreement in 1993 to ease tension along their frontier during a visit by former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao to Beijing.
In August 1995, India and China agreed to pull back their troops from four border posts in India's northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh, parts of which are claimed by China.

The agreement, one of four signed on Friday, stipulated that both sides would avoid large-scale military exercises involving more than one division of approximately 15,000 troops near the line of actual control.
"However, if such exercises are to be conducted, the strategic direction of the main force involved shall not be towards the other side," it added.
The agreement also said one side should inform the other through diplomatic channels if it planned combat aircraft flights within 10 km (six miles) from the line of control.

Officials said three other agreements signed on Friday were on preventing illegal drug trafficking, direct shipping links and an Indian consular office in Hong Kong after mid-1997 when China resumes sovereignty of the territory.
